IMPLEMENTATION / BOUNDARIES

Make every assumption visible.

What this version implements

Streaming stereo AudioWorklet processing at 44.1 kHz; measured two-ear horizontal KEMAR HRIR convolution; independent audiograms; NAL-R target gains; six broad overlapping bands; envelope-driven compression; ideal source directionality; added delay and direct-path blending; meters, local audio input and WAV export. The complete signal state remains alive between audio blocks.

The browser illustrations use frequency-dependent attenuation for reduced audibility. They are not MSBG, physiological models, or perceptual predictions. An offline Clarity MSBG experiment is included separately, together with a HASPI v2 feasibility pilot.

Why hearing loss is more than quieter sound

Outer-hair-cell dysfunction can reduce sensitivity, cochlear compression and frequency selectivity. Inner-hair-cell or neural dysfunction can reduce the information transmitted to the brain. Conductive and mixed losses have other mechanisms. A pure-tone audiogram does not uniquely identify these mechanisms. Amplification can improve access to sound, but cannot reconstruct missing sensory or neural coding.

Sources: NIDCD; Moore’s loudness-model review; Kates on compression.

Which frequencies are enhanced?

Gain depends on the audiogram and level, not a universal “best frequency.” We implement the NAL-R target rule at 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000 and 6000 Hz. A sloping profile often calls for more mid/high-frequency gain, but excessive high-frequency energy may add distortion or discomfort. Maximizing a waveform metric alone is not a fitting strategy.

Our band bank uses five one-pole lowpasses and differences, plus a highpass residual. Unity gains reconstruct the input exactly; unequal gains only approximate the target curve. Compression has a nominal 55 dB knee under an assumed 100 dB SPL per 0 dBFS mapping. That mapping is not headphone calibration. This is not NAL-NL2 and it is not clinical fitting software.

Are HRTFs used?

Yes, in this virtual scene: MIT KEMAR’s compact two-ear impulse responses, 128 taps at 44.1 kHz. We retain 37 horizontal directions from 0° to 180° and mirror ears for negative azimuth. Direction changes crossfade filter coefficients over 20 ms. These are generic anechoic ear responses, not individualized HRTFs or behind-the-ear microphone responses. Version 0.5 adds anthropometric scaling of KEMAR (head-width ITD scaling and frequency scaling) and custom full-circle sets converted from SOFA files; see the HRTF method.

A physical hearing aid already receives head-filtered microphone signals; it does not generally need to spatialize them again with an HRTF. HRTFs/BRIRs are useful for simulation and algorithm design; actual device geometry needs hearing-aid microphone transfer functions. For reverberation use room responses, not another head shadow on top of the same response.

Gardner & Martin / MIT KEMAR data and terms.

Echo cancellation versus feedback cancellation

Receiver sound can leak back into hearing-aid microphones, forming a closed acoustic feedback loop and producing instability. Adaptive feedback cancellation estimates and subtracts that path; correlation between desired speech and the receiver signal makes it challenging. This differs from vehicle/teleconference AEC, where a separately known loudspeaker reference is used to remove echo from microphone capture.

Version 0.5 implements that module: condition D closes a simulated receiver-to-microphone loop and compares plain NLMS, NLMS with frequency shifting and prediction-error-method AFC by maximum stable gain, convergence and wanted-sound level change. Plain NLMS is unstable for speech in quiet because of closed-loop bias; PEM-AFC is stable but attenuates steady tones. The path is synthetic and results are upper bounds for the model. See the feedback method. Vehicle-style AEC is still not implemented; added delay and direct blending remain separate open-fit illustrations.

Data and measurement

Two LibriSpeech test-clean files: 6930-75918-0000 and 6930-75918-0007. Both are from the same speaker. Audio is mono at source, normalized to 0.05 full-clip RMS for browser comparison and looped with short edge fades. Synthetic noise uses a fixed seed and first-order lowpass. The offline pilot instead uses white noise and calibrated numerical reference levels.

LibriSpeech is distributed by OpenSLR under CC BY 4.0. KEMAR requires attribution to Gardner & Martin. Asset hashes, exact identifiers, dependency versions and reproduction commands are included in the source package. User uploads and microphone audio are processed locally and are not transmitted by the application.

A final ±0.89 digital ceiling bounds samples. It does not set a safe acoustic SPL. Start with a low device volume and headphones; real hearing-aid gain requires calibration and professional fitting.

What is still required for a research comparison?

Real microphone-array beamforming, estimated localization, neural enhancement and source separation are literature candidates, not active processing modules here. There is no SOTA winner claimed. Hearing-impaired listener studies, hardware loopback timing, power profiling and a held-out multi-scene benchmark remain necessary.
